entries.literal: If the heir had been kept on the vessel by seniority and the mandate had not awaited the worthy, then hidden calamity would have dissolved of itself and the crisis could have been avoided.

entries.zh: 聖哲之訓，豈欺我哉！
entries.en: Can the teachings of the sages deceive us!
entries.literal: The teachings of the sages—can they deceive us!

entries.zh: 昔山濤舉羊祜為太子太傅，蓋欲以後事委之，而羊公短世。
entries.en: Formerly Shan Tao recommended Yang Hu as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, intending to entrust the succession to him, but Yang Hu died young.
entries.literal: Formerly Shan Tao recommended Yang Hu as Grand Tutor of the Heir Apparent, intending to entrust later affairs to him, but Lord Yang died young.

entries.zh: 僧綽綢繆主心，將任以國重，而宮車晏駕。
entries.en: Sengchuo had won the emperor's trust and was about to be entrusted with the weight of state, but the emperor died before he could take office.
entries.literal: Sengchuo had bound the ruler's heart and was about to be entrusted with the weight of the state, but the imperial carriage halted at dusk.

entries.zh: 二臣並以道德謙沖，名高兩代。
entries.en: Both men were alike in moral virtue and modest humility, renowned across two generations.
entries.literal: Both ministers were alike in moral virtue and modest humility, their fame high across two generations.

entries.zh: 胙未中年，功謝成日，惜矣哉！
entries.en: They had not reached midlife; their merit departed before its day—how regrettable!
entries.literal: Their blessings had not reached midlife; their merit departed before its day—how regrettable!

entries.zh: 初，太社西空地一區，吳時丁奉宅，孫晧流徙其家。
entries.en: A vacant plot west of the Grand Altar of Soil and Grain had been Ding Feng's residence in Wu times; Sun Hao exiled his household from it.
entries.literal: Earlier, a vacant plot west of the Grand Altar of Soil and Grain had been the residence of Ding Feng in Wu times; Sun Hao exiled his household from it.

entries.zh: 江左初為周顗、蘇峻宅，其後為袁悅宅，又為章武王司馬秀宅，皆以凶終。
entries.en: In the early years south of the Yangtze it had been the home of Zhou Yi and Su Jun; later of Yuan Yue, then of Prince Zhangwu Sima Xiu—all met violent ends.
entries.literal: In the early years south of the Yangtze it was the residence of Zhou Yi and Su Jun; afterward it was Yuan Yue's residence, then Prince of Zhangwu Sima Xiu's residence—all ended in violent death.

entries.zh: 後給臧燾，亦頗遇喪禍，故世稱為凶地。
entries.en: Later it was given to Zang Tao, who also suffered bereavement and disaster; the age therefore called it an ill-omened place.
entries.literal: Later it was given to Zang Tao, who also met with considerable bereavement and disaster; therefore the age called it an ill-omened place.

entries.zh: 僧綽常以正達自居，謂宅無吉凶，請以為第。
entries.en: Sengchuo, holding himself a man of upright character, maintained that dwellings had no luck or ill luck and asked to take it as his residence.
entries.literal: Sengchuo always set himself up as a man of upright attainment, held that dwellings had no luck or ill luck, and asked to take it as his residence.

entries.zh: 始就造築，未及居而敗。
entries.en: He had just begun building when, before he could move in, he met his downfall.
entries.literal: He had just begun construction and, before he could dwell there, met his downfall.

entries.zh: 子儉嗣，升明末，為齊國尚書右僕射。
entries.en: His son Jian succeeded; at the end of the Shengming era he was Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing in Qi.
entries.literal: His son Jian succeeded; at the end of the Shengming era he served as Right Vice Director of the Masters of Writing in the State of Qi.

entries.zh: 列傳第三十一 徐湛之江湛王僧綽
entries.en: Biography 31: Xu Zhanzhi, Jiang Zhan, and Wang Sengchuo
entries.literal: Biographies 31: Xu Zhanzhi, Jiang Zhan, and Wang Sengchuo

entries.zh: 義熙十二年，高祖北伐，有宋公之授，府遣一使慶殊命，參起居，延之與同府王參軍俱奉使至洛陽，道中作詩二首，文辭藻麗，為謝晦、傅亮所賞。
entries.en: In the twelfth year of Yixi (416), when the Founder Liu Yu campaigned north and received the title Duke of Song, the staff sent an envoy to mark the exceptional honor and attend court. Yanzhi and a fellow retainer named Wang went together to Luoyang; en route they wrote two poems whose diction was rich and polished, winning the praise of Xie Hui and Fu Liang.
entries.literal: In the twelfth year of Yixi, the Founder marched north; upon receiving investiture as Duke of Song, the office sent an envoy to celebrate the extraordinary appointment and attend to imperial audiences. Yanzhi and Wang, a staff retainer from the same office, were both sent as envoys to Luoyang. On the road they composed two poems; the language was ornate and splendid, and Xie Hui and Fu Liang admired them.

entries.zh: 宋國建，奉常鄭鮮之舉為博士，仍遷世子舍人。
entries.en: After the Song state was founded, Zheng Xianzhi, Director of Ceremonies, recommended him as Erudite, and he was soon transferred to Attendant of the Heir Apparent.
entries.literal: When the State of Song was established, Director of Ceremonies Zheng Xianzhi recommended him as Erudite; he was then moved to Attendant of the Heir Apparent.

entries.zh: 高祖受命，補太子舍人。
entries.en: When the Founder took the throne, Yanzhi was appointed Attendant of the Crown Prince.
entries.literal: When the Founder received the Mandate, he was appointed Attendant of the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 雁門人周續之隱居廬山，儒學著稱，永初中，徵詣京師，開館以居之。
entries.en: Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen, a celebrated Confucian recluse on Mount Lu, was summoned to the capital during Yongchu (420–422) and given a lecture hall to live in.
entries.literal: Zhou Xuzhi of Yanmen lived in seclusion on Mount Lu and was renowned in Confucian learning; during the Yongchu era he was summoned to the capital, and a hall was opened for him to dwell in.

entries.zh: 高祖親幸，朝彥畢至，延之官列猶卑，引升上席。
entries.en: The Founder came in person; the leading men of court were all present. Though Yanzhi still held a humble rank, he was brought to the seat of honor.
entries.literal: The Founder visited in person; court worthies all arrived. Yanzhi's official rank was still low, yet he was led up to the upper seat.

entries.zh: 上使問續之三義，續之雅仗辭辯，延之每折以簡要。
entries.en: The emperor set him to examine Xuzhi on the Three Meanings. Xuzhi leaned on his eloquence, but Yanzhi repeatedly cut him down with terse, pointed replies.
entries.literal: The emperor had him question Xuzhi on the Three Meanings; Xuzhi relied on his eloquence, and Yanzhi each time refuted him with brevity and precision.

entries.zh: 既連挫續之，上又使還自敷釋，言約理暢，莫不稱善。
entries.en: After he had repeatedly bested Xuzhi, the emperor had him explain his own views as well; his speech was spare yet lucid, and everyone praised him.
entries.literal: Having repeatedly defeated Xuzhi, the emperor also had him return and expound on his own; his words were concise and the reasoning clear, and none failed to praise him.

entries.zh: 徙尚書儀曹郎，太子中舍人。
entries.en: He was transferred to Gentleman of the Ministry of Rites and Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Crown Prince.
entries.literal: He was moved to Gentleman of the Ministry of Rites, and Attendant-in-Ordinary of the Crown Prince.

entries.zh: 元嘉三年，羨之等誅，徵為中書侍郎，尋轉太子中庶子，頃之，領步兵校尉，賞遇甚厚。
entries.en: In the third year of Yuanjia (426), after Xu Xianzhi and his faction were put to death, Yanzhi was recalled as Vice Director of the Secretariat, then made Vice Grandee of the Crown Prince's Household; soon he also served as Colonel of Footsoldiers and enjoyed lavish favor.
entries.literal: In the third year of Yuanjia, Xu Xianzhi and others were executed; he was summoned as Vice Director of the Secretariat, soon transferred to Vice Grandee of the Crown Prince's Household, and shortly after concurrently Colonel of Footsoldiers, with very generous rewards and favor.

entries.zh: 延之好酒疎誕，不能斟酌當世，見劉湛、殷景仁專當要任，意有不平，常云：「天下之務，當與天下共之，豈一人之智所能獨了！」
entries.en: Yanzhi drank heavily and was blunt and eccentric, ill suited to court the times. Seeing Liu Zhan and Yin Jingren monopolize power, he grew resentful and would say, "The empire's business should be the empire's business—can one man's wit settle it all?"
entries.literal: Yanzhi loved wine and was unrestrained and eccentric; he could not measure the present age. Seeing Liu Zhan and Yin Jingren monopolize key posts, he was discontent and often said: "The affairs of the realm ought to be shared with the realm—how can one man's wisdom finish them alone!"

entries.zh: 辭甚激揚，每犯權要。
entries.en: His language was fierce, and he repeatedly gave offense to men in power.
entries.literal: His words were very heated and exalted, and he often offended the powerful.

entries.zh: 謂湛曰：「吾名器不升，當由作卿家吏。」
entries.en: He told Liu Zhan, "My rank never rises—no doubt because I once served as a clerk in your household."
entries.literal: He said to Zhan: "My name and office do not rise—it must be because I served as your family's clerk."

entries.zh: 湛深恨焉，言於彭城王義康，出為永嘉太守。
entries.en: Zhan hated this deeply and spoke to Prince Yikang of Pengcheng; Yanzhi was sent out as Administrator of Yongjia.
entries.literal: Zhan deeply hated this and spoke to Prince of Pengcheng Yikang; he was sent out as Administrator of Yongjia.

entries.zh: 延之甚怨憤，乃作五君詠以述竹林七賢，山濤、王戎以貴顯被黜，詠嵇康曰：「鸞翮有時鎩，龍性誰能馴。」
entries.en: Burning with resentment, Yanzhi wrote his Odes to the Five Lords about the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, leaving out Shan Tao and Wang Rong as men who had risen to wealth and rank. Of Ji Kang he wrote: "A phoenix wing may be clipped in its season—who can tame a dragon's nature?"
entries.literal: Yanzhi was very resentful and angry, and composed Odes to the Five Lords to treat the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove; Shan Tao and Wang Rong were omitted for their noble prominence. On Ji Kang he wrote: "The phoenix pinion is sometimes clipped; who can tame a dragon's nature?"

entries.zh: 詠阮籍曰：「物故可不論，塗窮能無慟。」
entries.en: Of Ruan Ji: "When things are done with, why argue? When the road runs out, who does not mourn?"
entries.literal: On Ruan Ji: "When things are past one need not discuss them; when the road ends how can one not grieve?"

entries.zh: 詠阮咸曰：「屢薦不入官，一麾乃出守。」
entries.en: Of Ruan Xian: "Recommended again and again, yet never given office—a single gesture, and he is sent to rule a province."
entries.literal: On Ruan Xian: "Repeatedly recommended yet not entering office; one wave of the hand and he is sent out to govern."

entries.zh: 詠劉伶曰：「韜精日沉飲，誰知非荒宴。」
entries.en: Of Liu Ling: "Hoarding his spirit, he sinks daily into wine—who knows it is not a feast of despair?"
entries.literal: On Liu Ling: "Hiding his essence, daily drowning in drink—who knows it is not a wild feast?"

entries.zh: 此四句，蓋自序也。
entries.en: These four lines were plainly his own self-portrait.
entries.literal: These four lines were plainly his own self-account.

entries.zh: 湛及義康以其辭旨不遜，大怒。
entries.en: Zhan and Yikang, taking his verses as insolent, were furious.
entries.literal: Zhan and Yikang, because his words and intent were not deferential, were greatly enraged.

entries.zh: 時延之已拜，欲黜為遠郡，太祖與義康詔曰：「降延之為小邦不政，有謂其在都邑，豈動物情，罪過彰著，亦士庶共悉，直欲選代，令思愆里閭。
entries.en: Yanzhi had already accepted the post, but they meant to banish him to a remote commandery. Emperor Wen wrote to Yikang: "Sending Yanzhi to a minor post is not because he governs badly. Some say that in the capital he stirs people's hearts; his faults are plain and known to all. We only want to replace him and let him repent at home.
entries.literal: At that time Yanzhi had already received appointment; they wished to demote him to a distant commandery. Taizu instructed Yikang: "Demoting Yanzhi to a small state is not for poor governance—some say that in the capital he stirs men's feelings; his faults are conspicuous and known to gentlemen and commoners alike. We simply wish to choose a replacement and let him reflect on his errors in his home lane.

entries.zh: 猶復不悛，當驅往東土。
entries.en: If he still will not mend his ways, drive him to the eastern marches.
entries.literal: If he still does not reform, he should be driven to the eastern lands.

entries.zh: 乃志難恕，自可隨事錄治。
entries.en: If his intent is unforgivable, punish him as the case warrants.
entries.literal: If his will is hard to forgive, he may naturally be dealt with according to the matter on record.

entries.zh: 殷、劉意咸無異也。」
entries.en: Yin and Liu were of the same mind."
entries.literal: Yin and Liu's intentions were all the same."

entries.zh: 乃以光祿勳車仲遠代之。
entries.en: Che Zhongyuan, Director of the Imperial Household, was appointed in his stead.
entries.literal: Director of the Imperial Household Che Zhongyuan was made to replace him.

entries.zh: 延之與仲遠世素不協，屏居里巷，不豫人間者七載。
entries.en: Yanzhi and the Che family had long been at odds; he shut himself in his lane and kept out of public life for seven years.
entries.literal: Yanzhi and Zhongyuan had long been at odds by family tradition; he withdrew to his lane and did not take part in worldly affairs for seven years.

entries.zh: 中書令王球名公子，遺務事外，延之慕焉，球亦愛其材，情好甚款。
entries.en: Wang Qiu, Director of the Secretariat, was a celebrated nobleman's son who shunned office and lived apart; Yanzhi admired him, and Qiu in turn prized his talent—they became close friends.
entries.literal: Director of the Secretariat Wang Qiu was a famous nobleman's son who left affairs behind and dwelt apart; Yanzhi admired him, and Qiu also loved his talent—their affection was very warm.

entries.zh: 延之居常罄匱，球輒贍之。
entries.en: Yanzhi was often penniless at home; Qiu regularly supported him.
entries.literal: Yanzhi in his dwelling was often utterly destitute; Qiu would always supply him.

entries.zh: 晉恭思皇后葬，應須百官，湛之取義熙元年除身，以延之兼侍中。
entries.en: For the burial of Empress Gongsi of Jin, all officials were required to attend. Zhan dug up Yanzhi's appointment record from the first year of Yixi (405) and made him concurrent Attendant-in-Ordinary.
entries.literal: At the burial of Empress Gongsi of Jin, all officials were required; Zhan took the appointment document of the first year of Yixi and made Yanzhi concurrent Attendant-in-Ordinary.

entries.zh: 邑吏送札，延之醉，投札於地曰：「顏延之未能事生，焉能事死！」
entries.en: When the district clerk brought the summons, Yanzhi, drunk, flung it to the ground and said, "Yan Yanzhi could not serve the living—how should he serve the dead?"
entries.literal: The district clerk delivered the summons; Yanzhi was drunk and threw the summons to the ground, saying: "Yan Yanzhi could not serve the living—how could he serve the dead!"

entries.zh: :含生之氓，同祖一氣，等級相傾，遂成差品，遂使業習移其天識，世服沒其性靈。
entries.en: All who live share one breath of life; ranks press upon one another and form degrees, until habit shifts native understanding and worldly custom drowns the inborn spirit.
entries.literal: All living folk share one ancestral breath; ranks lean upon one another and thus form graded kinds, so that occupational habit shifts their heaven-given knowing and worldly garb drowns their native spirit.

entries.zh: 至夫願欲情嗜，宜無間殊，或役人而養給，然是非大意，不可侮也。
entries.en: Wishes and cravings ought not to differ in kind between men. Some employ others to feed themselves—yet this is no small matter and must not be treated lightly.
entries.literal: As for wishes, desires, feelings, and cravings—there ought to be no difference in kind. Some employ others to feed and supply themselves, yet this is not the great principle and must not be despised.

entries.zh: 隅奧有竈，齊侯蔑寒，犬馬有秩，管、燕輕饑。
entries.en: Even in a corner there is a stove; Duke Huan of Qi scorned the cold; dogs and horses have their stations; Guan Zhong and Yan Ying thought little of hunger.
entries.literal: In corner and recess there are stoves; the Marquis of Qi scorned cold; dogs and horses have order; Guan and Yan made light of hunger.

entries.zh: 若能服溫厚而知穿弊之苦，明周之德；
entries.en: If you can embrace warmth and plenty and know the pain of threadbare clothes, you understand the virtue of Zhou;
entries.literal: If one can submit to warmth and thickness and know the suffering of worn rags, one understands the virtue of Zhou;

entries.zh: 厭滋旨而識寡嗛之急，仁恕之功。
entries.en: if you tire of rich fare and know the urgency of plain food, you have achieved kindness and forbearance.
entries.literal: if one loathes rich flavors and knows the urgency of scant and frugal fare, this is the achievement of kindness and forbearance.

entries.zh: 豈與夫比肌膚於草石方手足於飛走者同其意用哉。
entries.en: How can that share the intent of those who compare flesh to grass and stone, or treat hands and feet like beasts' limbs?
entries.literal: How could this be the same intent and use as those who compare skin and flesh to grass and stone, or square hands and feet to flying and running beasts?

entries.zh: 罰慎其濫，惠戒其偏。
entries.en: In punishment guard against excess; in kindness guard against partiality.
entries.literal: In punishment be wary of excess; in favor be warned against partiality.

entries.zh: 罰濫則無以為罰，惠偏則不如無惠。
entries.en: When punishment runs wild it ceases to be punishment; when kindness is partial it is better to show none.
entries.literal: When punishment is excessive there is no longer punishment; when favor is partial it is better to have no favor.

entries.zh: 雖爾眇末，猶扁庸保之上，事思反己，動類念物，則其情得，而人心塞矣。
entries.en: Though you are slight, you still stand above the hired guard; in affairs turn back upon yourself, in action remember others' lot—then feeling is met and hearts are won.
entries.literal: Though you are minute and slight, you still stand above the common hired guard; in affairs think of turning back upon yourself, in movement constantly recall things—then their feeling is obtained and men's hearts are filled.

entries.zh: :覩驚異之事，或涉流傳；
entries.en: When one sees startling or strange things, one may get caught up in spreading them;
entries.literal: When one sees startling and strange matters, one may get involved in spreading them;

entries.zh: 遭卒迫之變，反思安順。
entries.en: when sudden crisis strikes, one then turns back to calm and obedience.
entries.literal: When one meets sudden and pressing change, one then reflects on peace and compliance.

entries.zh: 若異從己發，將尸謗人，迫而又迕，愈使失度。
entries.en: If the wonder springs from oneself, one will lay blame on others; pressed hard and at odds again, conduct loses all proper measure.
entries.literal: If the strangeness issues from oneself, one will lay slander on others; pressed and again at odds, one only makes conduct lose measure all the more.

entries.zh: 能夷異如裴楷，處逼如裴遐，可稱深士乎。
entries.en: To treat the strange as calmly as Pei Kai, to meet coercion as steadily as Pei Xia—can one be called a man of depth?
entries.literal: To level strangeness as Pei Kai did, to meet pressure as Pei Xia did—can one be called a profound person?

entries.zh: 閑居無事，為庭誥之文。
entries.en: In his leisure at home he wrote his Household Admonitions.
entries.literal: Living in retirement without affairs, he composed a text of Household Admonitions.

entries.zh: 今刪其繁辭，存其正，著于篇。
entries.en: Here the redundant passages are cut away and the essential passages retained for this chapter.
entries.literal: Now its redundant language is cut away and the essential kept, set down in this chapter.

entries.zh: 曰：
entries.en: It reads:
entries.literal: It says:

entries.zh: 元凶弒立，以為光祿大夫。
entries.en: When the usurper Liu Shao murdered his father and took the throne, Yanzhi was made Grand Master of Splendor.
entries.literal: When the usurper prince murdered and established himself, [Yanzhi] was made Grand Master of Splendor.

entries.zh: 先是，子竣為世祖南中郎諮議參軍。
entries.en: Earlier, his son Yan Jun had been Consulting Colonel on the Southern Staff of Emperor Xiaowu.
entries.literal: Before this, his son Jun had been Consulting Colonel of the Southern Staff to Emperor Xiaowu.

entries.zh: 及義師入討，竣參定密謀，兼造書檄。
entries.en: When the righteous army marched to punish the usurper, Jun took part in the secret plans and also drafted the proclamations.
entries.literal: When the righteous army entered to punish, Jun joined in fixing secret plans and also drafted the proclamations.

entries.zh: 劭召延之，示以檄文，問曰：「此筆誰所造﹖」延之曰：「竣之筆也。」
entries.en: Shao summoned Yanzhi, showed him the proclamation, and asked, "Whose hand wrote this?" Yanzhi said, "My son Jun's hand."
entries.literal: Shao summoned Yanzhi, showed him the proclamation document, and asked: "Whose brush made this?" Yanzhi said: "Jun's brush."

entries.zh: 又問：「何以知之﹖」延之曰：「竣筆體，臣不容不識。」
entries.en: He asked again, "How do you know?" Yanzhi said, "Jun's style of writing—your servant could not fail to know it."
entries.literal: He asked again: "How do you know?" Yanzhi said: "Jun's brush style—your servant could not fail to know."

entries.zh: 劭又曰：「言辭何至乃爾。」
entries.en: Shao also said, "How could the language go so far!"
entries.literal: Shao also said: "How could the words reach such a point!"

entries.zh: 延之曰：「竣尚不顧老父，何能為陛下。」
entries.en: Yanzhi said, "Jun does not even care for his aged father—how could he serve Your Majesty?"
entries.literal: Yanzhi said: "Jun does not even care for his old father—how could he do it for Your Majesty?"

entries.zh: 劭意乃釋，由是得免。
entries.en: Shao's suspicion was then lifted, and because of this Yanzhi was spared.
entries.literal: Shao's intent was then released; because of this he was spared.

entries.zh: 世祖登阼，以為金紫光祿大夫，領湘東王師。
entries.en: When Emperor Xiaowu came to the throne, Yanzhi was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon and concurrently Tutor to the Prince of Xiangdong.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xiaowu ascended the throne, he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon, and concurrently Tutor to the Prince of Xiangdong.

entries.zh: 子竣既貴重，權傾一朝，凡所資供，延之一無所受，器服不改，宅宇如舊。
entries.en: When his son Jun rose to power and swayed the court, Yanzhi accepted none of the provisions sent him; his furnishings and dress stayed as they were, his house unchanged.
entries.literal: His son Jun had already become noble and weighty, his power tilting the whole court; of all supplies offered, Yanzhi accepted none—his vessels and garments unchanged, his dwelling as before.

entries.zh: 常乘羸牛笨車，逢竣鹵簿，即屏往道側。
entries.en: He often rode a scrawny ox in a plain cart; whenever he met Jun's guard of honor, he would pull aside to the edge of the road.
entries.literal: He often rode a lean ox in a clumsy cart; when he met Jun's guard of honor, he would withdraw to the roadside.

entries.zh: 又好騎馬，遨游里巷，遇知舊輒據鞍索酒，得酒必頹然自得。
entries.en: He also loved to ride through the lanes; when he met old friends he would halt in the saddle and demand wine, and once he had it he would sink into contented ease.
entries.literal: He also loved riding horses and roaming lanes and alleys; meeting old acquaintances he would lean on the saddle and demand wine, and once he got wine he would always sink into satisfied abandon.

entries.zh: 常語竣曰：「平生不喜見要人，今不幸見汝。」
entries.en: He often told Jun, "All my life I have hated meeting the powerful—now, unhappily, I meet you."
entries.literal: He often told Jun: "All my life I have disliked meeting important men—now unhappily I meet you."

entries.zh: 竣起宅，謂曰：「善為之，無令後人笑汝拙也。」
entries.en: When Jun built a mansion, he told him, "Build it well—do not let posterity laugh at your lack of taste."
entries.literal: When Jun built a mansion, he said to him: "Build it well—do not let later men laugh at your clumsiness."

entries.zh: 表解師職，加給親信三十人。
entries.en: He memorialized to resign the tutorship and was granted thirty personal attendants in addition.
entries.literal: He memorialized to resign the tutorship and was given thirty personal attendants in addition.

entries.zh: 孝建三年，卒，時年七十三。
entries.en: In the third year of Xiaojian (456) he died at the age of seventy-three.
entries.literal: In the third year of Xiaojian (456), he died, aged seventy-three.

entries.zh: 追贈散騎常侍、特進，金紫光祿大夫如故。
entries.en: He was posthumously granted Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary and Special Advancement, while retaining his rank as Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
entries.literal: Posthumously he was given Regular Attendant-in-Ordinary and Special Advancement, with Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon as before.

entries.zh: 諡曰憲子。
entries.en: His posthumous title was Xianzi, "The Principled."
entries.literal: His posthumous title was Xianzi (The Principled).

entries.zh: 延之與陳郡謝靈運俱以詞彩齊名，自潘岳、陸機之後，文士莫及也，江左稱顏、謝焉。
entries.en: Yanzhi and Xie Lingyun of Chen were equally famed for literary brilliance; since Pan Yue and Lu Ji, no writer had matched them—the south spoke of Yan and Xie.
entries.literal: Yanzhi and Xie Lingyun of Chen commandery were both famed for equal brilliance in letters; since Pan Yue and Lu Ji, no man of letters could match them—the Eastern Jin called them Yan and Xie.

entries.zh: 所著並傳於世。
entries.en: His writings have all been handed down to posterity.
entries.literal: All that he wrote has been handed down in the world.

entries.zh: 史臣曰：出身事主，雖義在忘私，至於君親兩事，既無同濟，為子為臣，各隨其時可也。
entries.en: The historian writes: To leave home and serve a lord asks one to set private feeling aside; yet lord and parent are not duties one can fulfill together—as son and as minister, each must follow what the time permits.
entries.literal: The historian says: Leaving one's person to serve a lord—though righteousness lies in forgetting the private self—as for the two affairs of lord and parent, since they cannot be crossed together, to be son and to be minister, each follows what the time allows.

entries.zh: 若夫馳文道路，軍政恒儀，成敗所因，非繫乎此。
entries.en: As for dispatching proclamations on campaign and the fixed forms of civil and military rule, success and failure do not depend on that.
entries.literal: As for dispatching writings on the road and the constant forms of military and civil affairs—the causes of success and failure do not hang on this.

entries.zh: 而據筆數罪，陵讎犯逆，餘彼慈親，垂之虎吻，以此為忠，無聞前誥。
entries.en: Yet to take up the brush and list crimes, to revile the enemy and denounce rebellion, abandoning one's loving father and delivering him to the tiger's maw—to call that loyalty finds no warrant in the admonitions of old.
entries.literal: Yet to take up the brush and count crimes, to insult the foe and denounce rebellion, leaving aside that kindly parent and handing him to the tiger's maw—calling this loyalty has no hearing in former admonitions.

entries.zh: 夫自忍其親，必將忍人之親，自忘其孝，期以申人之孝，食子放鹿，斷可識矣。
entries.en: He who can harden himself against his own parent will harden himself against others' parents; he who forgets his own filial duty expects to fulfill others'—as with Yi Ya who cooked his son, or Duke Huan who freed the deer, the pattern is plain.
entries.literal: One who can bear against his own parent will surely bear against others' parents; one who forgets his own filial piety expects to extend others' filial piety—Yi Ya who ate his son and Duke Huan who released the deer: this can clearly be known.

entries.zh: 記云：「八十者一子不從政，九十者家不從政。」
entries.en: The Record says: "At eighty, one son is excused from office; at ninety, the whole household is excused."
entries.literal: The Record says: "When a man is eighty, one son does not enter government; when he is ninety, the household does not enter government."

entries.zh: 豈不以年薄桑榆，憂患將及，雖有職王朝，許以辭事，況顛沛之道，慮在未測者乎。
entries.en: Is it not because when years draw near sunset, trouble is at hand, one may hold office at court yet be allowed to withdraw—and how much more on a path of turmoil, when what lies ahead cannot be foreseen?
entries.literal: Is it not because years approach mulberry and elm dusk, calamity and worry are about to arrive—though one holds office at the royal court, one is permitted to resign affairs; how much more on a road of hardship and turmoil, when concern lies in what cannot be foreseen?

entries.zh: 自非延年之辭允而義愜，夫豈或免。
entries.en: Had Yannian's words not been apt and his conduct not justified, how could he have escaped?
entries.literal: Unless Yannian's words were fitting and his righteousness satisfying, how could he have escaped?

entries.zh: 元嘉九年，至京邑，以為黃門侍郎，累遷江夏內史。
entries.en: In the ninth year of Yuanjia he reached the capital, was appointed Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, and rose step by step to Interior Minister of Jiangxia.
entries.literal: In the ninth year of Yuanjia he reached the capital and was made Gentleman of the Yellow Gate, then was promoted repeatedly to Interior Minister of Jiangxia.

entries.zh: 雍州刺史劉道產卒，羣蠻大動，脩之為征西司馬討蠻，失利。
entries.en: After Liu Daochan, Inspector of Yongzhou, died, the tribal peoples stirred on a large scale. Xiuzhi served as Western Campaigning Marshal against them but met defeat.
entries.literal: When Inspector of Yongzhou Liu Daochan died, the tribal peoples rose in great numbers. Xiuzhi served as Western Campaigning Marshal and attacked the tribes but was defeated.

entries.zh: 孝武初，為寧蠻校尉、雍州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: Early in Emperor Xiaowu's reign he was made Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou, with overall military authority.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaowu's reign he was made Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou, with overall command added.

entries.zh: 脩之在政寬簡，士眾悅附。
entries.en: His rule was easy and unassuming; soldiers and officials gladly attached themselves to him.
entries.literal: In his administration Xiuzhi was lenient and simple; officers and men were glad to follow him.

entries.zh: 及荊州刺史南郡王義宣反，檄脩之舉兵，脩之偽與之同，而遣使陳誠於帝。
entries.en: When Yixuan, Prince of Nanjun and Inspector of Jingzhou, rebelled, he called on Xiuzhi to join the revolt. Xiuzhi feigned agreement while sending an envoy to pledge his loyalty to the throne.
entries.literal: When the Inspector of Jingzhou, the Prince of Nanjun Yixuan, rebelled, he summoned Xiuzhi to raise troops. Xiuzhi pretended to agree while sending an envoy to declare his loyalty to the emperor.

entries.zh: 帝嘉之，以為荊州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: The emperor commended him and appointed him Inspector of Jingzhou with overall military authority.
entries.literal: The emperor praised him and made him Inspector of Jingzhou with overall command.

entries.zh: 義宣聞脩之不與己同，乃以魯秀為雍州刺史，擊襄陽。
entries.en: Learning that Xiuzhi would not stand with him, Yixuan named Lu Xiu Inspector of Yongzhou and marched on Xiangyang.
entries.literal: When Yixuan learned that Xiuzhi would not join him, he appointed Lu Xiu Inspector of Yongzhou and attacked Xiangyang.

entries.zh: 脩之命斷馬鞍山道，秀不得前，乃退。
entries.en: Xiuzhi had the Ma'an Mountain route blocked; Xiu could not get through and retreated.
entries.literal: Xiuzhi ordered the Ma'an Mountain road cut; Xiu could not advance and withdrew.

entries.zh: 及義宣敗於梁山，單舟南走，脩之率眾南定遺寇。
entries.en: After Yixuan was beaten at Liangshan and fled south alone by boat, Xiuzhi led his troops south to subdue the scattered rebels.
entries.literal: When Yixuan was defeated at Liangshan and fled south in a lone boat, Xiuzhi led his forces south to pacify the remnant bandits.

entries.zh: 時竺超民執義宣，脩之至，乃殺之，以功封南昌縣侯。
entries.en: Zhu Chaomin then held Yixuan captive. Xiuzhi arrived, killed Yixuan, and for this service was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nanchang county.
entries.literal: At that time Zhu Chaomin held Yixuan prisoner. When Xiuzhi arrived he killed Yixuan and, for his merit, was enfeoffed as Marquis of Nanchang.

entries.zh: 三十年，孝武伐元凶，以慤為南中郎諮議參軍，領中兵。
entries.en: In the thirtieth year, when Emperor Xiaowu marched against the deposed heir Yuanxiong, Que served as advising officer on the Southern General of the Household's staff and commanded the central troops.
entries.literal: In the thirtieth year, when Emperor Xiaowu attacked the deposed heir Yuanxiong, Que was made advising staff officer of the Southern Palace Attendant and commanded the central guard.

entries.zh: 孝武即位，以為左衞將軍，封洮陽侯，功次柳元景。
entries.en: After Xiaowu's accession, Que was made General of the Left Guard and enfeoffed as Marquis of Taoyang; his merit stood just below Liu Yuanying's.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xiaowu took the throne, Que was made General of the Left Guard and enfeoffed as Marquis of Taoyang, his merit ranking just after Liu Yuanying's.

entries.zh: 孝建中，累遷豫州刺史，監五州諸軍事。
entries.en: During the Xiaojian reign he rose step by step to Inspector of Yuzhou, supervising military affairs across five provinces.
entries.literal: During the Xiaojian era he was promoted repeatedly to Inspector of Yuzhou and overseer of military affairs in five provinces.

entries.zh: 先是，鄉人庾業，家甚富豪，方丈之膳，以待賓客，而慤至，設以菜葅粟飯，謂客曰：「宗軍人，慣噉粗食。」
entries.en: Earlier, his townsman Yu Ye had been enormously rich, setting feasts that filled a square zhang for his guests. When Que visited, Ye served only pickles and millet gruel, telling the company, "Commander Zong is a soldier—he is accustomed to plain fare."
entries.literal: Earlier, his fellow townsman Yu Ye was extremely wealthy. His meals for guests filled a square zhang, yet when Que came he set out pickled vegetables and millet rice and told the guests, "Commander Zong is a military man—he is used to coarse food."

entries.zh: 慤致飽而去。
entries.en: Que ate his fill and departed.
entries.literal: Que ate his fill and left.

entries.zh: 至是業為慤長史，帶梁郡，慤待之甚厚，不以前事為嫌。
entries.en: By then Ye served as Que's chief administrator with concurrent authority over Liang Commandery, and Que treated him with great kindness, bearing no grudge for the old slight.
entries.literal: By then Ye was Que's chief administrator with concurrent command of Liang Commandery, and Que treated him very generously, taking no offense at the past.

entries.zh: 尋復為豫州刺史。
entries.en: Before long he was reappointed Inspector of Yuzhou.
entries.literal: Soon he was again made Inspector of Yuzhou.

entries.zh: 淮上亡命司馬黑石推立夏侯方進為主，改姓李名弘，以惑眾，玄謨討斬之。
entries.en: A Huai River outlaw, Sima Heishi, proclaimed Xia Houfangjin leader, styled him Li Hong to beguile the people; Xuanmo crushed the band and executed him.
entries.literal: On the Huai a fugitive named Sima Heishi set up Xia Houfangjin as leader, changed his surname to Li and his name to Hong, to delude the masses; Xuanmo attacked and beheaded him.

entries.zh: 遷寧蠻校尉、雍州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: He was moved to Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou with overall authority.
entries.literal: He was transferred to Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou with overall command.

entries.zh: 雍土多僑寓，玄謨請土斷流民，當時百姓不願屬籍，罷之。
entries.en: Yongzhou held many displaced households. Xuanmo petitioned to register wandering populations locally; the people resisted enrollment and the policy was dropped.
entries.literal: Yong had many sojourners; Xuanmo asked to fix native registers for the floating population. The people then did not wish to be entered on the rolls, and the measure was abandoned.

entries.zh: 其年，玄謨又令九品以上租，使貧富相通，境內莫不嗟怨。
entries.en: That same year he levied rent even on men of the ninth rank and above, forcing rich and poor to share alike; the whole province groaned in protest.
entries.literal: That year Xuanmo also ordered rent from men of the ninth rank and above, forcing rich and poor to share the burden; throughout the commandery none did not sigh in resentment.

entries.zh: 民間訛言玄謨欲反，時柳元景當權，元景弟僧景為新城太守，以元景之勢，制令南陽、順陽、上庸、新城諸郡並發兵討玄謨。
entries.en: Word ran that Xuanmo meant to rebel. Liu Yuanying then dominated the court; his brother Sengjing governed Xincheng and, leaning on Yuanying's power, ordered Nanyang, Shunyang, Shangyong, Xincheng, and neighboring commanderies to march against Xuanmo.
entries.literal: Rumors spread that Xuanmo would rebel. Liu Yuanying then held power; Yuanying's younger brother Sengjing was Administrator of Xincheng and, relying on Yuanying's influence, ordered Nanyang, Shunyang, Shangyong, Xincheng, and other commanderies all to raise troops against Xuanmo.

entries.zh: 玄謨令內外晏然，以解眾惑，馳啟孝武，具陳本末。
entries.en: Xuanmo kept his household and camp unruffled to quiet rumor and rushed a full account to Emperor Xiaowu.
entries.literal: Xuanmo ordered inner and outer calm to dispel the people's doubts and sent a swift report to Emperor Xiaowu, setting out the whole story.

entries.zh: 帝知其虛，馳遣主書吳喜公撫慰之，又答曰：「梁山風塵，初不介意，君臣之際，過足相保，聊復為笑，伸卿眉頭。」
entries.en: Knowing the accusation hollow, the emperor dispatched Chief Clerk Wu Xigong to reassure him and wrote back, "The turmoil at Liangshan never troubled me. Between sovereign and minister we have more than enough trust—come, let us laugh again and smooth your brow."
entries.literal: The emperor knew the charge was false and sent Chief Clerk Wu Xigong posthaste to comfort him, replying also, "The dust of Liangshan—I never minded it. Between lord and minister we have more than enough to trust one another. Let us laugh again and unknit your brow."

entries.zh: 玄謨性嚴，未嘗妄笑，時人言玄謨眉頭未曾伸，故帝以此戲之。
entries.en: Stern by nature, he seldom smiled; people said his brow had never relaxed—hence the emperor's jest.
entries.literal: Xuanmo was stern by nature and never laughed lightly. Men of the time said his brow had never unknit; hence the emperor jested thus.

entries.zh: 後為金紫光祿大夫，領太常。
entries.en: He later became Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with golden seal and purple ribbon, while also heading the Ministry of Rites.
entries.literal: Later he was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with the golden seal and purple ribbon, and headed the Ministry of Rites.

entries.zh: 及建明堂，以本官領起部尚書，又領北選。
entries.en: When the Bright Hall was raised, he kept his rank, headed the ministry overseeing its construction, and supervised northern appointments.
entries.literal: When the Bright Hall was built, he retained his title and also headed the Ministry for Hall Construction and northern selection of officials.

entries.zh: 孝武狎侮羣臣，隨其狀貌，各有比類，多鬚者謂之羊。
entries.en: Emperor Xiaowu bullied his ministers and mocked their faces with nicknames—men with heavy beards he called "goats."
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaowu treated his ministers familiarly and insultingly, matching each to his looks with a nickname: the bearded he called "goat."

entries.zh: 顏師伯缺齒，號之曰齴。
entries.en: Yan Shibo was missing teeth; they nicknamed him "Gummy."
entries.literal: Yan Shibo lacked teeth; he was dubbed "gummy."

entries.zh: 劉秀之儉吝，呼為老慳。
entries.en: Liu Xiuzhi was tight-fisted; they called him "Old Miser."
entries.literal: Liu Xiuzhi was miserly; they called him "old skinflint."

entries.zh: 黃門侍郎宗靈秀體肥，拜起不便，每至集會，多所賜與，欲其瞻謝傾踣，以為歡笑。
entries.en: Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Zong Lingxiu was obese and clumsy at court bows. At every feast the emperor showered him with gifts, hoping he would trip when he rose to thank him and provide a laugh.
entries.literal: Gentleman of the Yellow Gate Zong Lingxiu was corpulent and awkward in bowing and rising. At every gathering the emperor gave him many gifts, wishing that when he looked up to give thanks he would stumble and fall for laughter.

entries.zh: 又刻木作靈秀父光祿勳叔獻像，送其家廳事。
entries.en: He even had a wooden statue carved of Lingxiu's father, Superintendent of the Imperial Household Shuxian, and sent it to their reception hall.
entries.literal: He also carved a wooden image of Lingxiu's father, the Superintendent of the Imperial Household Shuxian, and sent it to their family hall.

entries.zh: 柳元景、垣護之並北人，而玄謨獨受「老傖」之目。
entries.en: Liu Yuanying and Yuan Huzhi were northerners too, yet only Xuanmo was tagged "Old Barbarian."
entries.literal: Liu Yuanying and Yuan Huzhi were both northerners, yet Xuanmo alone bore the label "old barbarian."

entries.zh: 凡所稱謂，四方書疏亦如之。
entries.en: Whatever nicknames he coined, correspondence from every quarter repeated them.
entries.literal: Whatever names he gave, letters from the four directions used them likewise.

entries.zh: 嘗為玄謨作四時詩曰：「菫荼供春膳，粟漿充夏飡。
entries.en: He once wrote Xuanmo a poem on the four seasons: "Shepherd's purse for spring fare; millet broth for summer meals.
entries.literal: He once composed a four-season poem for Xuanmo, saying, "Shepherd's purse supplies the spring meal; millet gruel fills the summer board.

entries.zh: 瓟醬調秋菜，白醝解冬寒。」
entries.en: Gourd paste dresses autumn greens; rice wine lees ward off winter chill."
entries.literal: Gourd sauce seasons autumn greens; white lees break winter's cold."

entries.zh: 又寵一崐崘奴子，名白主。
entries.en: He also doted on a Kunlun slave boy named Baizhu ("White Master").
entries.literal: He also favored a Kunlun slave boy named Baizhu.

entries.zh: 常在左右，令以杖擊羣臣，自柳元景以下，皆罹其毒。
entries.en: Baizhu stayed always at his side, and the emperor had him beat the ministers with a staff—from Liu Yuanying downward, all felt his blows.
entries.literal: He kept him always at his side and ordered him to strike the ministers with a staff; from Liu Yuanying down, all suffered at his hands.

entries.zh: 大明三年，竟陵王誕據廣陵反，慤表求赴討，乘驛詣都，面受節度，上停輿慰勉，慤聳躍數十，左右顧盻，上壯之。
entries.en: In the third year of Daming, the Prince of Jingling, Dan, rebelled at Guangling. Que petitioned to lead the suppression, raced by post relay to the capital, and received his commission face to face. The emperor stopped his carriage to exhort him. Que sprang up and down dozens of times, looking about him; the emperor was stirred.
entries.literal: In the third year of Daming, the Prince of Jingling, Dan, held Guangling in revolt. Que memorialized asking to go to suppress him, rode post-horses to the capital, and received orders in person. The emperor halted his carriage to encourage him. Que leapt several tens of times, glancing left and right; the emperor was impressed.

entries.zh: 及行，隸車騎大將軍沈慶之。
entries.en: On campaign he served under Shen Qingzhi, Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry.
entries.literal: On the march he was placed under the Grand General of Chariots and Cavalry Shen Qingzhi.

entries.zh: 初，誕誑其眾云：「宗慤助我。」
entries.en: At first Dan had deceived his men, saying, "Zong Que is on my side."
entries.literal: At first Dan had deceived his troops, saying, "Zong Que is helping me."

entries.zh: 及慤至，躍馬繞城呼曰：「我宗慤也。」
entries.en: When Que arrived he galloped around the walls crying, "I am Zong Que!"
entries.literal: When Que arrived he spurred his horse around the walls and shouted, "I am Zong Que!"

entries.zh: 事平，入為左衞將軍。
entries.en: After the rebellion was crushed he returned to court as General of the Left Guard.
entries.literal: When the affair was settled he entered the capital as General of the Left Guard.

entries.zh: 五年，從獵墮馬，脚折不堪朝直，以為光祿大夫，加金紫。
entries.en: In the fifth year he fell from his horse while hunting, broke his leg, and could no longer attend court. He was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with the golden seal and purple ribbon.
entries.literal: In the fifth year, while hunting he fell from his horse and broke his leg, unable to attend court. He was made Grand Master of Splendid Happiness with the golden seal and purple ribbon added.

entries.zh: 慤有佳牛堪進御，官買不肯賣，坐免官。
entries.en: Que owned an excellent ox suitable for presentation to the throne. When officials sought to purchase it he refused to sell and was removed from his post.
entries.literal: Que had a fine ox fit to present to the throne. When the authorities wished to buy it he would not sell and was dismissed from office.

entries.zh: 明年，復職。
entries.en: The following year he was reappointed.
entries.literal: The next year he was restored to office.

entries.zh: 廢帝即位，為寧蠻校尉、雍州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: When the Deposed Emperor acceded, Que was made Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou with overall military authority.
entries.literal: When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Que was made Colonel Pacifying the Tribes and Inspector of Yongzhou with overall command.

entries.zh: 卒，贈征西將軍，諡曰肅侯。
entries.en: At his death he was posthumously made General Who Pacifies the West; his posthumous title was Marquis Su ("Solemn").
entries.literal: When he died he was posthumously made General Who Pacifies the West; his posthumous title was Marquis Su.

entries.zh: 泰始二年，詔以慤配食孝武廟。
entries.en: In the second year of Taishi an edict granted him a place in the sacrifices at Emperor Xiaowu's ancestral temple.
entries.literal: In the second year of Taishi an edict ordered that Que receive offerings in Emperor Xiaowu's temple.

entries.zh: 子羅雲，卒，子元寶嗣。
entries.en: His son Luoyun died; the title passed to his grandson Yuanbao.
entries.literal: His son Luoyun died; his grandson Yuanbao succeeded.

entries.zh: 時虜攻陷滑臺，執朱脩之以歸。
entries.en: At that time the enemy stormed Huatai and carried Zhu Xiuzhi off captive.
entries.literal: At that time the barbarians attacked and took Huatai, carrying Zhu Xiuzhi away.

entries.zh: 玄謨上疏曰：「王途始開，隨復淪塞，非惟天時，抑亦人事。
entries.en: Xuanmo submitted a memorial: "The imperial highway has only just been reopened, yet it is blocked again—not by season alone, but by human failure.
entries.literal: Xuanmo submitted a memorial saying, "The royal road has only just opened, yet it is again lost and blocked—this is not heaven's season alone but also human affairs.

entries.zh: 虎牢、滑臺，豈惟將之不良，抑亦本之不固。
entries.en: For Hulao and Huatai, was the fault only in the generals, or also in weak foundations?
entries.literal: Hulao and Huatai—was it only that the generals were poor, or also that the foundations were not firm?

entries.zh: 本之不固，皆由民憚遠役。
entries.en: Weak foundations come from the people's dread of distant service.
entries.literal: When the foundations are not firm, it is because the people dread distant corvée.

entries.zh: 臣請以西陽之魯陽，襄陽之南鄉，發甲卒，分為兩道，直趣淆、澠，征士無遠徭之思，吏士有屢休之歌。
entries.en: I propose drafting soldiers from Luyang in Xiyang and Nanxiang in Xiangyang, splitting them into two columns to drive straight on Xiao and Mian, so conscripts need not fear distant levy and troops may enjoy real respite.
entries.literal: Your servant asks to mobilize armor-bearers from Luyang in Xiyang and Nanxiang in Xiangyang, divide them into two columns, and strike straight for Xiao and Mian, so that the drafted soldiers feel no thought of far-off service and officers and men have songs of repeated rest.

entries.zh: 若欲以東國之眾，經營牢、洛，道途既遠，獨克實難。」
entries.en: If you mean to move the eastern provinces' manpower against Hulao and Luoyang, the distances are great and victory would be hard to win alone."
entries.literal: If you wish to use the masses of the eastern domains to operate on Hulao and Luoyang, the roads are long and success alone would be hard."

entries.zh: 玄謨每陳北侵之策，上謂殷景仁曰：「聞王玄謨陳說，使人有封狼居胥意。」
entries.en: Whenever Xuanmo pressed plans for northern invasion, the emperor told Yin Jingren, "Hearing Wang Xuanmo speak always stirs in me the ambition of enfeoffing Wolf Mountain."
entries.literal: Each time Xuanmo urged a northern campaign, the emperor told Yin Jingren, "When I hear Wang Xuanmo's proposals I feel the will to enfeoff Wolf Mountain."

entries.zh: 後為興安侯義賓輔國司馬、彭城太守。
entries.en: He was later made staff officer to the Pacifying State for Marquis of Xing'an Yibin and Administrator of Pengcheng.
entries.literal: Later he was made Pacifying-State staff officer to the Marquis of Xing'an, Yibin, and Administrator of Pengcheng.

entries.zh: 義賓薨，玄謨上表，以彭城要兼水陸，請以皇子撫臨州事，乃以孝武出鎮。
entries.en: After Yibin's death, Xuanmo memorialized that Pengcheng was crucial by land and water and asked that a prince govern the province; Emperor Xiaowu was then sent to take command.
entries.literal: When Yibin died, Xuanmo submitted a memorial that Pengcheng was vital on land and water and asked that a prince oversee the province. Thereupon Emperor Xiaowu was sent to hold the post.

entries.zh: 元凶弒立，玄謨為冀州刺史。
entries.en: After the heir Yuanxiong murdered his father and seized the throne, Xuanmo was appointed Inspector of Jizhou.
entries.literal: When the deposed heir murdered his way to the throne, Xuanmo was made Inspector of Jizhou.

entries.zh: 孝武伐逆，玄謨遣濟南太守垣護之將兵赴義。
entries.en: When Emperor Xiaowu marched to punish the usurper, Xuanmo sent Jinan Administrator Yuan Huzhi with troops to join the loyal side.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xiaowu marched against the usurper, Xuanmo sent the Administrator of Jinan, Yuan Huzhi, with troops to aid the righteous cause.

entries.zh: 事平，除徐州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: After the revolt was crushed he became Inspector of Xuzhou with overall military authority.
entries.literal: When the affair was settled he was made Inspector of Xuzhou with overall command.

entries.zh: 及南郡王義宣與江州刺史臧質反，朝庭假玄謨輔國將軍，拜豫州刺史，與柳元景南討，軍屯梁山，夾岸築偃月壘，水陸待之。
entries.en: When Yixuan, Prince of Nanjun, and Jiangzhou Inspector Zang Zhi rose in revolt, the court named Xuanmo acting Pacifying-State General and Inspector of Yuzhou. With Liu Yuanying he marched south, encamped at Liangshan, and threw up crescent ramparts on both riverbanks to meet the rebels by land and water.
entries.literal: When the Prince of Nanjun, Yixuan, and the Inspector of Jiangzhou, Zang Zhi, rebelled, the court made Xuanmo acting Pacifying-State General and Inspector of Yuzhou, and with Liu Yuanying marched south to attack. The army encamped at Liangshan and built crescent ramparts along both banks to await them by land and water.

entries.zh: 義宣遣劉諶之就臧質，陳軍城南，玄謨留老弱守城，悉精兵接戰，賊遂大潰。
entries.en: Yixuan sent Liu Shenzhi to Zang Zhi's camp. The rebels drew up south of the city. Xuanmo left the aged and weak to guard the walls and led every able man to the fight; the enemy collapsed.
entries.literal: Yixuan sent Liu Shenzhi to join Zhi. They arrayed their army south of the city. Xuanmo left the old and weak to hold the town and led all his picked troops to battle; the rebels were utterly routed.

entries.zh: 加都督、前將軍，封曲江縣侯。
entries.en: He received overall command and the rank of Forward General and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qujiang.
entries.literal: Overall command and the post of Forward General were added; he was enfeoffed as Marquis of Qujiang.

entries.zh: 中軍司馬劉沖之白孝武，言：「玄謨在梁山，與義宣通謀。」
entries.en: Central Army staff officer Liu Chongzhi reported to Emperor Xiaowu, saying, "At Liangshan, Xuanmo was secretly colluding with Yixuan."
entries.literal: Central Army staff officer Liu Chongzhi reported to Emperor Xiaowu, saying, "At Liangshan, Xuanmo was in secret league with Yixuan."

entries.zh: 上意不能明，使有司奏玄謨多取寶貨，虛張戰簿，與徐州刺史垣護之並免官。
entries.en: The emperor could not judge the charge clearly. He had officials report that Xuanmo had seized great spoils and falsified battle records; both he and Xuzhou Inspector Yuan Huzhi were dismissed.
entries.literal: The emperor could not see clearly. He had the authorities memorialize that Xuanmo had taken many treasures and inflated battle rolls, and both he and Xuzhou Inspector Yuan Huzhi were removed from office.

entries.zh: 孝武崩，與柳元景等俱受顧命，以外監事委玄謨。
entries.en: At Xiaowu's death he and Liu Yuanying and others received the final testament; border affairs were placed in Xuanmo's hands.
entries.literal: When Emperor Xiaowu died, he and Liu Yuanying and others alike received the dying charge; foreign affairs were entrusted to Xuanmo.

entries.zh: 時朝政多門，玄謨以嚴直不容，徙青、冀二州刺史，加都督。
entries.en: Court factions multiplied; Xuanmo's stern integrity could not be borne, and he was shifted to Inspector of Qing and Ji with overall command.
entries.literal: Government then had many factions; Xuanmo's stern uprightness could not be tolerated, and he was moved to Inspector of Qing and Ji with overall command.

entries.zh: 少帝既誅顏師伯、柳元景等，狂悖益甚，以領軍徵玄謨。
entries.en: After the Deposed Emperor killed Yan Shibo, Liu Yuanying, and the rest, his madness deepened. He recalled Xuanmo as General of the Palace Guard.
entries.literal: After the Deposed Emperor had executed Yan Shibo, Liu Yuanying, and others, his frenzy grew worse. He summoned Xuanmo as General of the Palace Guard.

entries.zh: 子姪咸勸稱疾，玄謨曰：「吾受先帝厚恩，豈可畏禍苟免。」
entries.en: Sons and nephews begged him to feign sickness. Xuanmo said, "The late emperor favored me deeply—how could I shrink from peril and save myself?"
entries.literal: His sons and nephews all urged him to plead illness. Xuanmo said, "I received deep grace from the late emperor—how could I fear disaster and seek an easy escape?"

entries.zh: 遂行。
entries.en: He went.
entries.literal: He set out.

entries.zh: 及至，屢表諫諍，又流涕請緩刑去殺，以安元元。
entries.en: On reaching court he remonstrated again and again, weeping as he begged that executions be slowed and slaughter ended so the people might be calmed.
entries.literal: When he arrived he memorialized repeatedly in remonstrance and, weeping, begged that punishments be eased and killings stopped to settle the common people.

entries.zh: 少帝大怒。
entries.en: The Deposed Emperor flew into a rage.
entries.literal: The Deposed Emperor was greatly enraged.

entries.zh: 玄謨幼而不羣，世父蕤有知人鑒，常笑曰：「此兒氣概高亮，有太尉彥雲之風。」
entries.en: Xuanmo was wild even as a boy. His uncle Rui, who could read character well, would laugh and say, "The lad's bearing is high and bright—he has something of Grand Commandant Yan Yun about him."
entries.literal: Xuanmo was unruly from boyhood. His father's elder brother Rui had a gift for judging men and would often laugh, saying, "This boy's spirit is lofty and bright; he has the air of Grand Commandant Yan Yun."

entries.zh: 武帝臨徐州，辟為從事史，與語異之。
entries.en: When Emperor Wu held Xuzhou he summoned Xuanmo as an attendant clerk and, in conversation, found him remarkable.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu was in Xuzhou he summoned him as an attendant clerk and, speaking with him, found him unusual.

entries.zh: 少帝末，謝晦為荊州，請為南蠻行參軍、武寧太守。
entries.en: Near the end of Emperor Shaodi's reign, Xie Hui governed Jingzhou and took him on as acting staff officer for the southern tribes and as Defender of Wuning.
entries.literal: At the end of Emperor Shaodi's reign, Xie Hui was in Jingzhou and invited him as Southern Tribes Acting Staff Officer and Defender of Wuning.

entries.zh: 晦敗，以非大帥見原。
entries.en: When Hui fell, Xuanmo was spared because he had not been a principal commander.
entries.literal: When Hui was defeated, because Xuanmo had not been a chief commander he was pardoned.

entries.zh: 元嘉中，補長沙王義欣鎮軍中兵參軍，領汝陰太守。
entries.en: During Yuanjia he was appointed staff officer in the central army of the Prince of Changsha, Yixin, while also serving as Administrator of Ruyin.
entries.literal: In the Yuanjia era he was made Central Army staff officer to the Prince of Changsha, Yixin, with concurrent office as Administrator of Ruyin.

entries.zh: 朱脩之
entries.en: Zhu Xiuzhi
entries.literal: Zhu Xiuzhi

entries.zh: 太宗即位，改督為都督，進號安東將軍，太守如故。
entries.en: When Emperor Ming took the throne, Zi Fang's supervisory command was elevated to full commandership, he was promoted to General Who Pacifies the East, and he retained his post as governor.
entries.literal: When Emperor Ming acceded, his command was changed from supervisor to commander-in-chief, he was advanced to General Who Pacifies the East, and his governorship was unchanged.

entries.zh: 又徵為撫軍，領太常。
entries.en: He was also recalled to serve as General Who Pacifies the Army and concurrently as Minister of Rites.
entries.literal: He was also summoned as General Who Pacifies the Army and concurrently headed the Ministry of Rites.

entries.zh: 長史孔覬不受命，舉兵反，應晉安王。
entries.en: Chief Administrator Kong Xian refused to obey, raised troops in revolt, and rallied to Jin'an Prince.
entries.literal: Chief Administrator Kong Xian refused the order, raised troops in rebellion, and responded to Jin'an Prince.

entries.zh: 子勛即偽位，進子房號車騎將軍、開府儀同三司。
entries.en: When Zi Xun took the rebel throne, he promoted Zi Fang to General of Chariots and Cavalry with privileges equal to the Three Excellencies.
entries.literal: When Zi Xun took the false throne, he advanced Zi Fang's title to General of Chariots and Cavalry with an establishment equal to the Three Excellencies.

entries.zh: 三吳晉陵並受命於覬。
entries.en: The Three Wu commanderies and Jinling all submitted to Kong Xian's authority.
entries.literal: The Three Wu regions and Jinling all accepted orders from Xian.

entries.zh: 太宗遣衞將軍巴陵王休若督諸將吳喜等東討，戰無不捷，以次平定。
entries.en: Emperor Ming sent Guards General Prince of Baling Xiu Ruo to lead generals including Wu Xi in an eastern campaign. They won every battle and pacified the region step by step.
entries.literal: Emperor Ming sent Guards General Prince of Baling Xiu Ruo to command the generals Wu Xi and others in an eastern campaign; in battle they were never unsuccessful, and the regions were pacified in succession.

entries.zh: 上虞令王晏起兵殺覬，囚子房，送還京都，上宥之，貶為松滋縣侯，食邑千戶。
entries.en: Shangyu Magistrate Wang Yan raised troops, killed Kong Xian, imprisoned Zi Fang, and sent him to the capital. The Emperor spared his life but demoted him to Marquis of Songzi with a fief of one thousand households.
entries.literal: Magistrate of Shangyu Wang Yan raised troops, killed Xian, imprisoned Zi Fang, and sent him back to the capital; the Emperor pardoned him and demoted him to Marquis of Songzi county with a fief of one thousand households.

entries.zh: 大明七年生，仍封東平王，食邑二千戶。
entries.en: Born in the seventh year of Daming, he was at once made Prince of Dongping with a fief of two thousand households.
entries.literal: He was born in the seventh year of Daming and was at once enfeoffed as Prince of Dongping with a fief of two thousand households.

entries.zh: 繼東平沖王休倩。
entries.en: He succeeded Dongping Chong Prince Xiu Qian as heir.
entries.literal: He succeeded Dongping Chong Prince Xiu Qian.

entries.zh: 休倩母顏性理嚴酷，泰始二年，子嗣所生母景寧園昭容謝上表曰：「故東平沖王休倩託荄璿極，岐嶷夙表，降年弗永，遺胤莫傳。
entries.en: Xiu Qian's mother Yan was by nature harsh and cruel. In the second year of Taishi, Zi Si's birth mother Lady Xie, Attendant of Jingning Garden, submitted a memorial: "The late Dongping Chong Prince Xiu Qian was entrusted to the imperial house, showed keen intelligence from youth, but died young and left no heir.
entries.literal: Xiu Qian's mother Yan was by nature stern and cruel. In the second year of Taishi, Zi Si's birth mother, Lady Xie, Attendant of Jingning Garden, submitted a memorial, saying: "The late Dongping Chong Prince Xiu Qian was entrusted to the jade axis of the pole, showed early keen intelligence, but his descending years were not long and left no heir to transmit the line.

entries.zh: 孝武皇帝敕妾子臣子嗣出繼為後，既承國祀，方奉烝薦，庶覃遐慶，式延于遠。
entries.en: Emperor Xiaowu ordered my son Zi Si to be given in adoption as his successor. Having received the state's sacrifices, he was just beginning to offer the seasonal rites, hoping to spread blessing far into the future.
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaowu ordered my son the subject Zi Si to go out in adoption as successor; having received the state's sacrifices, he was just offering the seasonal offerings, hoping to spread distant blessing and extend it far.

entries.zh: 而妾顏訓養非恩，撫導乖理，情闕引進，義違負螟。
entries.en: Yet Lady Yan's nurturing was not kind, her guidance contrary to reason, her affection failing to nurture him, her conduct violating the duty owed to an adopted son.
entries.literal: Yet the lady Yan's nurturing was not gracious, her guidance contrary to reason, affection lacking in advancement, duty violated like abandoning the locust larva.

entries.zh: 昔世祖平日，詭申慈愛；
entries.en: In former days, during the Emperor's lifetime, she only pretended affection;
entries.literal: In former days, during the Emperor's ordinary times, she falsely displayed affection;

entries.zh: 崩背未幾，真性便發，猶逼畏崇憲，少欲藏掩。
entries.en: not long after his death her true nature emerged, yet still constrained by fear of Empress Dowager Chongxian, she tried somewhat to conceal it.
entries.literal: not long after his death her true nature burst forth, yet still constrained by fear of Empress Dowager Chongxian, she wished somewhat to conceal it.

entries.zh: 自茲以後，專縱嚴酷，實顯布宗戚，宣灼宮闈，用傷人倫，爰惻行路。
entries.en: From then on she indulged solely in harsh cruelty, displaying it openly among the imperial kin and throughout the inner palace, wounding human decency and moving all who heard to pity.
entries.literal: From then on she indulged solely in severity and cruelty, truly displaying it among the imperial kin, proclaiming it throughout the inner palace, thereby wounding human relations and moving passersby to pity.

entries.zh: 妾天屬冥至，感切實深，伏願乾渥廣臨，曲垂照賜，復改命還依本屬，則妾母子雖隕之辰，猶生之年。」
entries.en: Your servant's kin has reached the dark realm, and my grief cuts deep. I prostrate myself hoping for your broad favor: change the command and let him return to his original status. Then for mother and son, though we face ruin, it would still be as though we lived."
entries.literal: Your servant's heaven-bound kin has reached the dark realm; the feeling cuts truly deep. We prostrate ourselves hoping for broad imperial favor and bending grace, that the command be changed and he return to his original status; then for your servant mother and son, though the hour of falling, it would still be a day of life."

entries.zh: 許之。
entries.en: The request was granted.
entries.literal: It was granted.

entries.zh: 其年賜死，時年四歲。
entries.en: That year he was ordered to take his own life. He was four at the time.
entries.literal: That year he was granted death; he was then four years old.

entries.zh: 孝武帝二十八男：文穆皇后生廢帝子業、豫章王子尚，陳淑媛生晉安王子勛，阮容華生安陸王子綏，徐昭容生皇子子深，何淑儀生松滋侯子房，史昭華生臨海王子頊，殷貴妃生始平孝敬王子鸞，次永嘉王子仁，與皇子子深同生，何婕妤生皇子子鳳，謝昭容生始安王子真，江婕妤生皇子子玄，史昭儀生邵陵王子元，次齊敬王子羽，與始平孝敬王子鸞同生，江美人生皇子子衡，楊婕妤生淮南王子孟，次皇子子況，與皇子子玄同生，次南平王子產，與永嘉王子仁同生，次晉陵孝王子雲，次皇子子文，並與始平孝敬王子鸞同生，次廬陵王子輿，與淮南王子孟同生，次南海哀王子師，與始平孝敬王子鸞同生，次淮陽思王子霄，與皇子子玄同生，次皇子子雍，與始安王子真同生，次皇子子趨，與皇子子鳳同生，次皇子子期，與皇子子衡同生，次東平王子嗣，與始安王子真同生，杜容華生皇子子悅。
entries.en: Emperor Xiaowu had twenty-eight sons. Empress Wenmu bore the Deposed Emperor Ziye and Yuzhang Prince Zi Shang. Lady Chen bore Jin'an Prince Zi Xun. Ruan Ronghua bore Anlu Prince Zi Sui. Xu Zhaorong bore Prince Zi Shen. He Shuyi bore Songzi Marquis Zi Fang. Shi Zhaohua bore Linhai Prince Zi Xu. Noble Consort Yin bore Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan, then Yongjia Prince Zi Ren (twins with Prince Zi Shen). Lady He bore Prince Zi Feng. Xie Zhaorong bore Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen. Lady Jiang bore Prince Zi Xuan. Lady Shi bore Shaoling Prince Zi Yuan, then Qi Jing Prince Zi Yu (twins with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan). Lady Jiang bore Prince Zi Heng. Lady Yang bore Huainan Prince Zi Meng, then Prince Zi Kuang (twins with Prince Zi Xuan), then Nanping Prince Zi Chan (twins with Yongjia Prince Zi Ren), then Jinling Xiao Prince Zi Yun and Prince Zi Wen (all twins with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan), then Luling Prince Zi Yu (twins with Huainan Prince Zi Meng), then Nanhai Ai Prince Zi Shi (twins with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan), then Huaiyang Si Prince Zi Xiao (twins with Prince Zi Xuan), then Prince Zi Yong (twins with Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen), then Prince Zi Qu (twins with Prince Zi Feng), then Prince Zi Qi (twins with Prince Zi Heng), then Dongping Prince Zi Si (twins with Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen). Du Ronghua bore Prince Zi Yue.
entries.literal: Emperor Xiaowu had twenty-eight sons: Empress Wenmu bore the Deposed Emperor Ziye and Yuzhang Prince Zi Shang; Lady Chen bore Jin'an Prince Zi Xun; Ruan Ronghua bore Anlu Prince Zi Sui; Xu Zhaorong bore Prince Zi Shen; He Shuyi bore Songzi Marquis Zi Fang; Shi Zhaohua bore Linhai Prince Zi Xu; Noble Consort Yin bore Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan, next Yongjia Prince Zi Ren, born together with Prince Zi Shen; Lady He bore Prince Zi Feng; Xie Zhaorong bore Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen; Lady Jiang bore Prince Zi Xuan; Lady Shi bore Shaoling Prince Zi Yuan, next Qi Jing Prince Zi Yu, born together with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan; Lady Jiang bore Prince Zi Heng; Lady Yang bore Huainan Prince Zi Meng, next Prince Zi Kuang, born together with Prince Zi Xuan, next Nanping Prince Zi Chan, born together with Yongjia Prince Zi Ren, next Jinling Xiao Prince Zi Yun, next Prince Zi Wen, all born together with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan, next Luling Prince Zi Yu, born together with Huainan Prince Zi Meng, next Nanhai Ai Prince Zi Shi, born together with Shiping Xiaojing Prince Zi Luan, next Huaiyang Si Prince Zi Xiao, born together with Prince Zi Xuan, next Prince Zi Yong, born together with Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen, next Prince Zi Qu, born together with Prince Zi Feng, next Prince Zi Qi, born together with Prince Zi Heng, next Dongping Prince Zi Si, born together with Shi'an Prince Zi Zhen; Du Ronghua bore Prince Zi Yue.

entries.zh: 安陸王子綏、南平王子產、廬陵王子輿並出繼。
entries.en: Anlu Prince Zi Sui, Nanping Prince Zi Chan, and Luling Prince Zi Yu were all given in adoption to continue other lines.
entries.literal: Anlu Prince Zi Sui, Nanping Prince Zi Chan, and Luling Prince Zi Yu were all adopted out as heirs.

entries.zh: 皇子子深、子鳳、子玄、子衡、子況、子文、子雍未封，早夭。
entries.en: Princes Zi Shen, Zi Feng, Zi Xuan, Zi Heng, Zi Kuang, Zi Wen, and Zi Yong were never enfeoffed and died in childhood.
entries.literal: Princes Zi Shen, Zi Feng, Zi Xuan, Zi Heng, Zi Kuang, Zi Wen, and Zi Yong received no fiefs and died young.

entries.zh: 子趨、子期、子悅未封，為明帝所殺。
entries.en: Zi Qu, Zi Qi, and Zi Yue had received no fiefs when Emperor Ming had them put to death.
entries.literal: Zi Qu, Zi Qi, and Zi Yue received no fiefs and were killed by Emperor Ming.

entries.zh: 顧覬之，字偉仁，吳郡吳人也。
entries.en: Gu Jizhi, whose style was Weiren, came from Wu in Wu commandery.
entries.literal: Gu Jizhi, style name Weiren, was a man of Wu in Wu commandery.

entries.zh: 高祖謙，字公讓，晉平原內史陸機姊夫。
entries.en: His great-grandfather Qian, whose style was Gongrang, was the brother-in-law of Lu Ji, Interior Governor of Pingyuan under Jin.
entries.literal: His great-grandfather Qian, style name Gongrang, was brother-in-law to Lu Ji, Jin Interior Governor of Pingyuan.

entries.zh: 祖崇，大司農。
entries.en: His grandfather Chong had served as Director of the Grand Granary.
entries.literal: His grandfather Chong was Director of the Grand Granary.

entries.zh: 父黃老，司徒左西掾。
entries.en: His father Huanglao had served as Left Western Aide to the Chief Minister.
entries.literal: His father Huanglao was Left Western Aide to the Chief Minister.

entries.zh: 覬之初為郡主簿。
entries.en: Jizhi began his career as chief clerk of his commandery.
entries.literal: Jizhi first served as commandery chief clerk.

entries.zh: 謝晦為荊州，以為南蠻功曹，仍為晦衛軍參軍。
entries.en: When Xie Hui was posted to Jingzhou, he appointed Jizhi Merit Officer for the Southern Man and then staff officer on Hui's Guard Army.
entries.literal: When Xie Hui held Jingzhou, he made him Merit Officer for the Southern Man and then staff officer on Hui's Guard Army.

entries.zh: 晦愛其雅素，深相知待。
entries.en: Hui admired his refined simplicity and treated him with deep trust and regard.
entries.literal: Hui loved his refined simplicity and treated him with deep mutual regard.

entries.zh: 王弘辟為揚州主簿，仍為弘衛軍參軍，鹽官令，衡陽王義季右軍主簿，尚書都官郎，護軍司馬。
entries.en: Wang Hong recruited him as chief clerk of Yangzhou, then as staff officer on Hong's Guard Army, magistrate of Yanguan, Right Army chief clerk to Prince Yiji of Hengyang, an officer in the Secretariat's capital-crimes section, and Protecting Army marshal.
entries.literal: Wang Hong recruited him as Yangzhou chief clerk, then as Hong's Guard Army staff officer, magistrate of Yanguan, Right Army chief clerk to Prince of Hengyang Yiji, Secretariat Officer in the Capital Crimes section, and Protecting Army marshal.

entries.zh: 時大將軍彭城王義康秉權，殷、劉之隙已著，覬之不欲與殷景仁久接事，乃辭腳疾自免歸。
entries.en: At the time Grand General Prince Yikang of Pengcheng held power, and the rift between Yin Jingren and Liu Yilong was already open. Jizhi did not wish to serve alongside Yin Jingren and pleaded a foot ailment to resign and return home.
entries.literal: At the time the Grand General, Prince of Pengcheng Yikang, held power; the rift between Yin and Liu was already manifest; Jizhi did not wish to serve long with Yin Jingren and so pleaded foot ailment to resign and return home.

entries.zh: 在家每夜常于床上行腳，家人竊異之，而莫曉其意。
entries.en: At home he would walk about on his bed each night. His family found this strange but none understood his purpose.
entries.literal: At home each night he would often walk his feet upon the bed; the household privately found it strange but none understood his intent.

entries.zh: 後義康徙廢，朝廷多以異同受禍。
entries.en: Later, when Yikang was demoted and disgraced, many at court suffered ruin for their political affiliations.
entries.literal: Later Yikang was demoted and disgraced; many at court suffered calamity for their affiliations.

entries.zh: 復為東遷、山陰令。
entries.en: He again served as magistrate of Dongqian and Shanyin in succession.
entries.literal: He again served as magistrate of Dongqian and Shanyin.

entries.zh: 山陰民戶三萬，海內劇邑，前後官長，晝夜不得休，事猶不舉。
entries.en: Shanyin had thirty thousand households and was among the most demanding counties in the realm. Successive magistrates worked day and night without rest, yet still could not keep up with their duties.
entries.literal: Shanyin had thirty thousand households, a commandery of the greatest difficulty within the realm; successive magistrates could not rest day or night, yet affairs still went unaccomplished.

entries.zh: 覬之理繁以約，縣用無事，晝日垂簾，門階閑寂。
entries.en: Jizhi governed complexity through simplicity. The county ran without incident; by day he let the curtain hang down, and his gate and courtyard stood quiet and still.
entries.literal: Jizhi governed complexity through simplicity; the county had no troubles; by day he let the curtain hang and the gate and steps were quiet and still.

entries.zh: 自宋世為山陰，務簡而績修，莫能尚也。
entries.en: From the Song period onward, no magistrate of Shanyin had matched his combination of simple administration and well-ordered achievement.
entries.literal: From the Song era as magistrate of Shanyin, his affairs were simple yet his achievements well ordered—none could surpass him.

entries.zh: 還為揚州治中從事史，廣陵王誕、廬陵王紹北中郎左司馬，揚州別駕從事史，尚書吏部郎。
entries.en: He returned to serve as Senior Clerk of Yangzhou, Northern Central Left Staff Officer to Princes Dan of Guangling and Shao of Luling, Vice Director of Yangzhou, and an officer in the Secretariat's civil-service section.
entries.literal: He returned as Yangzhou Senior Clerk, Northern Central Left Staff Officer to Princes of Guangling Dan and of Luling Shao, Yangzhou Vice Director, and Secretariat Officer in the Civil Service section.

entries.zh: 嘗于太祖坐論江左人物，言及顧榮，袁淑謂覬之曰：「卿南人怯懦，豈辦作賊。」
entries.en: Once, at a gathering of Taizu discussing figures of the Jiang left, Gu Rong's name came up. Yuan Shu said to Jizhi, "You southerners are timid and weak—how could you ever manage to be rebels?"
entries.literal: Once at a gathering of Taizu discussing figures of the Jiang left, when Gu Rong was mentioned Yuan Shu said to Jizhi: "You southerners are timid and weak—how could you manage to be rebels?"

entries.zh: 覬之正色曰：「卿乃複以忠義笑人！」
entries.en: Jizhi replied with a stern face, "You would mock a man for his loyalty and righteousness!"
entries.literal: Jizhi with stern countenance said: "You would mock a man for his loyalty and righteousness!"

entries.zh: 淑有愧色。
entries.en: Shu looked ashamed.
entries.literal: Shu showed a look of shame.

entries.zh: 對曰：子可謂扶繩而辨，循刻而議。
entries.en: He replied: You may be said to argue by holding the rope of the argument and to debate by following the sundial's shadow—your reasoning is exacting indeed.
entries.literal: The reply came: You may be said to argue by holding a rope and to debate by following a marking on the sundial.

entries.zh: 若乃宣攝有方，豈非吉運所屬；
entries.en: As for regulating and governing with proper method—is that not the province of fortunate destiny?
entries.literal: As for regulating and governing with proper method—is that not what fortunate destiny belongs to?

entries.zh: 將迎有會，實亦凶數自挻。
entries.en: That meeting has its occasion is true; yet ill-fated numbers also extend themselves of their own accord.
entries.literal: That meeting has its occasion is true; yet ill-fated numbers also extend themselves.

entries.zh: 若夫陽施陰德，長世遐年，揆厥所原，孰往非命。
entries.en: As for active benevolence and hidden virtue, long generations and distant years—when one traces them to their origin, where does anything go that is not fate?
entries.literal: As for yang-bestowal and yin-virtue, long generations and distant years—when one traces them to their origin, where does anything go that is not fate?

entries.zh: 研復來旨，讎校往說，起予惟商，未識所異。
entries.en: I have studied your latest meaning and collated it with earlier discourse. You enlighten me—I can discuss with you, yet I do not see where we differ.
entries.literal: I have studied your latest meaning and collated it with earlier discourse; you enlighten me—I can discuss with you, yet I do not see where we differ.

entries.zh: 資生稟運，參差萬殊，逆順吉凶，理數不一。
entries.en: The endowment of life and received fortune vary among ten thousand differences; rebellion and obedience, good and ill, follow principles and numbers that are not one.
entries.literal: The endowment of life and received fortune vary among ten thousand differences; rebellion and obedience, good and ill, follow principles and numbers that are not one.

entries.zh: 原夫餐椒非養生之術，咀劍豈衛性之經。
entries.en: For eating pepper is not a method of nourishing life, and chewing swords is hardly a canon for guarding one's nature.
entries.literal: For eating pepper is not a method of nourishing life, and chewing swords is hardly a canon for guarding one's nature.

entries.zh: 命之所延，人肉其骨，而含嚼膏粱，時或嬰患。
entries.en: Where fate extends life, one may eat human flesh to the bone—yet those who chew rich grains still sometimes contract illness.
entries.literal: Where fate extends life, one eats human flesh to the bone—yet those who chew rich grains still sometimes contract illness.

entries.zh: 深澗乖徼寵之津，空谷絕探榮之轍，運之所集，物稊其枯，而俯仰竿牘，終然離沮。
entries.en: Deep ravines lack paths to favor; empty valleys cut off tracks to glory—where fortune gathers, things wither to dryness, while those who bow and rise with brush and document still end in separation and dejection.
entries.literal: Deep ravines miss the ford of favor; empty valleys cut off tracks of seeking glory—where fortune gathers, things wither to dryness, while those who bow and rise with brush and document still end in separation and dejection.

entries.zh: 爾乃蹻、蹠橫行；
entries.en: Then Bo Yi and Robber Zhi go unrestrained;
entries.literal: Then Bo Yi and Robber Zhi go unrestrained;

entries.zh: 曾、原窘步。
entries.en: Zeng Shen and Yan Yuan walk in distress.
entries.literal: Zeng Shen and Yan Yuan walk in distress.

entries.zh: 湯、周延世，詡、邑絕緒。
entries.en: Tang and Zhou extended their lines through generations; Xu You and Boyi ended without posterity.
entries.literal: Tang and Zhou extended their generations; Xu and Yi ended their lines.

entries.zh: 吉凶征應，糾纆若茲。
entries.en: The omens of good and ill fortune correspond, tangled together thus.
entries.literal: The omens of good and ill correspond, tangled together thus.

entries.zh: 畢萬保軀，宓賤喪領，梁野之言，豈不或妄。
entries.en: Bi Wan preserved his body, Mi Zijian lost his head—are Liang Yi's words not perhaps mistaken?
entries.literal: Bi Wan preserved his body, Mi Zijian lost his head—are Liang Yi's words not perhaps mistaken?

entries.zh: 谷南、魯北，甘此促生；
entries.en: South of the valley, north of Lu—they willingly accept this shortened span of life;
entries.literal: South of the valley, north of Lu—they willingly accept this shortened life;

entries.zh: 彭翁、竇叟，將以何術。
entries.en: Old Peng and Old Dou—by what arts did they do it?
entries.literal: Old Peng, Old Dou—by what arts?

entries.zh: 晉平、趙敬，淫放已該；
entries.en: Duke Ping of Jin and King Jing of Zhao were licentious and dissolute to the full;
entries.literal: Duke Ping of Jin and King Jing of Zhao—licentious and dissolute, already complete;

entries.zh: 漢主、魏相，奚獨傷夭。
entries.en: The Han emperor and the Wei minister—why did they alone die young?
entries.literal: The Han lord and the Wei minister—why alone die young?

entries.zh: 同異若斯，是非孰正。
entries.en: Similarities and differences like these—which view is right and which wrong?
entries.literal: Similarities and differences like these—which is right and which wrong?

entries.zh: 至如雷濱凝分，挫志遠圖；
entries.en: As when at Lei Ford the streams congealed and parted, frustrating ambitions for distant achievement;
entries.literal: As when at Lei Ford the streams congealed and parted, frustrating ambitions for distant achievement;

entries.zh: 棘津陰拱，振功高世。
entries.en: while at Jiji Ford one waited in hidden stillness and shook the age with lofty merit.
entries.literal: while at Jiji Ford one waited in hidden stillness and shook the age with lofty merit.

entries.zh: 樊生沖矯，鐫旌善之文，華子高抗，銘懲非之策，皆士衡所雲「同川而異歸」者也。
entries.en: Fan Sheng strove upward and engraved words praising the good; Hua Zi stood high in opposition and inscribed policies warning against evil—all examples of what Lu Ji called "the same stream yet different destinations."
entries.literal: Fan Sheng strove upward and engraved words praising the good; Hua Zi stood high in opposition and inscribed policies warning against evil—all examples of what Lu Ji called "the same stream yet different destinations."

entries.zh: 殊塗均致，實繁有征。
entries.en: Different paths reach the same end—instances of this are indeed numerous and verified.
entries.literal: Different paths reach the same end—instances of this are indeed numerous and verified.

entries.zh: 即理易推，在言可略。
entries.en: Following from principle one can easily infer; in words it may be brief.
entries.literal: Following from principle one can easily infer; in words it may be brief.

entries.zh: 昔兩都全盛，六合殷昌，霧集貴寵之閭，雲動權豪之術，鈞貿貽談，豈唯陳、張而已。
entries.en: In former days when both capitals were in full splendor and the realm prospered, mist gathered in lanes of noble favor and clouds stirred in wards of powerful magnates—tales of equal standing were handed down; was it only Chen Ping and Zhang Liang?
entries.literal: In former days when both capitals were in full splendor and the realm prospered, mist gathered in lanes of noble favor and clouds stirred in wards of powerful magnates—tales of equal price in trade were handed down; was it only Chen and Zhang?

entries.zh: 觀夫二子，才未越眾，而此以藉榮揮價，彼獨擯景淪聲，通否之運，斷可知矣。
entries.en: Considering these two men, their talent did not surpass the multitude, yet one rode borrowed glory to raise his price while the other alone was cast into shadow and sank in repute—the fortune of passage or obstruction can clearly be known.
entries.literal: Considering these two men, their talent did not surpass the multitude, yet one rode borrowed glory to raise his price while the other alone was cast into shadow and sank in repute—the fortune of passage or obstruction can clearly be known.

entries.zh: 嚴、辛不安時任命，而委罪亮直，亦地脈之徒歟。
entries.en: Yan Jun and Xin Ping did not rest content with their allotted times and appointments, yet blamed the straight and bright—is this also the cohort of those who talk of underground veins?
entries.literal: Yan and Xin did not rest content with their allotted times and appointments, yet blamed the straight and bright—is this also the cohort of those who talk of underground veins?

entries.zh: 若神仙所序，顯明修習，齊強燕平，厥驗未著，李覃董芬，其效安在。
entries.en: As for what immortals set forth and bright cultivation—Qi was strong, Yan was pacified, yet their verification did not appear; Li Tan and Dong Fen—where are their effects?
entries.literal: As for what immortals set forth and bright cultivation—Qi was strong, Yan was pacified, yet their verification did not appear; Li Tan and Dong Fen—where are their effects?

entries.zh: 喬、松之侶，雲飛天居，夷、列之徒，風行水息，良由理數懸挺，實乃鐘茲景命。
entries.en: Companions of Wang Qiao and Chi Songzi soar through clouds and dwell in heaven; followers of Boyi and Liezi move with the wind and rest upon the water—truly because principle and number stand far apart, they in fact received this splendid destiny.
entries.literal: Companions of Qiao and Song soar through clouds and dwell in heaven; followers of Boyi and Liezi move with the wind and rest upon the water—truly because principle and number stand far apart, they in fact received this splendid destiny.

entries.zh: 天竺遺文，星華方策，因造前定，果報指期，貧豪莫差，修夭無爽，有允瑣辭，無愆鄙說，統而言之，孰往非命。
entries.en: India's transmitted texts and the star-flowered cubic charts establish prior determination; karmic retribution points to its term; poor and great are not differentiated, long life and early death are not in error; there are trustworthy petty phrases and no fault in humble discourse—unified in speech, where does anything go that is not fate?
